posts.topic: Seam allowance: what it is, checking it, sewing it accurately

slides.title: Seam allowance, explained in 3 simple steps
slides.subtitle: That little strip between the stitching and the edge decides whether your garment fits. Here's how to get it right.

slides.title: Know what it is
slides.body: Seam allowance is the distance between your stitching line and the cut edge of the fabric. Sew wider or narrower than planned and the whole garment changes size.

slides.title: Check your pattern first
slides.body: Before you cut, read the instructions to see how much seam allowance is included. Some patterns add it for you, others ask you to add it yourself.

slides.title: Sew it accurately
slides.body: Line the fabric edge up with the matching line on your machine's needle plate. Watch the guide, not the needle, and sew slowly round curves.

slides.title: Save this for sewing day
slides.body: Every Pattern Perfection pattern tells you the seam allowance and walks you through each seam step by step.

posts.caption_ig:
If your finished garment came out a little too big or too small, the seam allowance might be the culprit 🪡

Swipe for 3 steps to master it: know what it is, check how much your pattern includes, and sew it accurately using the guide on your needle plate.

A tiny difference on every seam adds up fast, so it's worth getting right.

1️⃣ Know what it is: the distance from stitching line to cut edge
2️⃣ Check how much your pattern includes before cutting
3️⃣ Follow the guide on your needle plate, not the needle

posts.topic: Cutting napped and directional fabrics in one direction

slides.title: Velvet or one-way prints? Cut one way
slides.body: Velvet, corduroy and directional prints look different upside down. Lay every pattern piece pointing the same way before you cut.

posts.caption_ig:
Ever finished a project and noticed one panel looks a shade darker? 🤔

Velvet, corduroy and other fabrics with a pile (called nap) reflect light differently depending on direction. One-way prints can end up upside down too.

The fix: lay every pattern piece with its top pointing the same way before you cut ✂️ It uses a bit more fabric, so buy a little extra.

Save this for your autumn velvet and cord projects 🍂

#sewingtips #fabric #sewingforbeginners #sewinghacks #isew
posts.caption_fb:
Quick fabric tip for autumn sewing 🍂

Velvet, corduroy and one-way prints change colour or direction depending on how you cut them. Lay all your pattern pieces with the top pointing the same way, and buy a little extra fabric to allow for it.

Have you ever been caught out by a shiny-then-dull velvet panel? 😅

slides.title: How to lengthen or shorten a pattern
slides.subtitle: Your size fits but the length doesn't? It's one of the easiest adjustments to make before you cut.

slides.title: Compare the lengths
slides.body: Measure your back waist length or a garment you love and compare it with the pattern. XS to XL charts assume a standard height.

slides.title: Use the adjustment lines
slides.body: Cut along the lengthen or shorten line. To add length, spread the pieces and tape paper behind. To remove length, fold out an even tuck.

slides.title: Redraw the side seams
slides.body: Your seams will now have a little step. Join the edges with a smooth line, then repeat the same change on every matching piece.

slides.title: Sew it to your length
slides.body: Our patterns come in sizes XS to XL with US and UK sizing and clear step-by-step instructions.

posts.caption_ig:
Right size, wrong length? You don't need a different pattern, just a 5-minute adjustment 📏

Swipe to see how: compare the lengths, use the lengthen/shorten line, then redraw your seams.

Standard sizing (like US and UK XS–XL) assumes an average height, so petite and tall sewists often tweak the length. It's completely normal.
